Dear Tarun,
You asked how the presenting is going. Honestly? Last month, after my first client pitch, I sat in the washroom and told myself, "I can't do this. Some people just can't speak in front of others."
Then I remembered what you used to say when we were learning to code: "Not yet." So I tried it. I can't present well yet. It sounded silly, but it changed the question from "what's wrong with me" to "what do I try next."
And the answer wasn't just "practise more." I'd practised plenty, reading my slides out loud to the wall. So I changed the method. I recorded myself on the phone, cut my slides from twenty to eight, and asked Meenal from the next team to throw hard questions at me.
Yesterday's pitch wasn't perfect. But I didn't hide in the washroom after.
Write back soon,
Rafiq

qa.a: Rafiq felt defeated and ashamed, hiding in the washroom and thinking some people just can't speak in front of others.

"You want the swimming story, Kavitha? Fine. I'm Tarun, I'm twenty-five, and until last year I couldn't swim at all.
The first class, I stood in the shallow end with eight-year-olds, and I swallowed half the pool. I went home and said, 'I can't swim. I never will. It's too late for me.'
My sister said, 'You can't swim yet.' I rolled my eyes. But the word stuck. It made me ask a different question. Not 'why am I useless' but 'what do I try next?'
And trying harder didn't work. I thrashed for three weeks and got nowhere. So I changed things. I asked the coach for one-to-one sessions. I practised floating only, for a whole week, before any strokes.
In March I swam one full length. Badly. But one full length.
So now when something feels impossible, I say 'yet,' and then I ask what to change."

qa.q: What did Tarun practise for a whole week before any strokes?
qa.a: Tarun practised floating only.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel after the first swimming class?
qa.a: Tarun felt hopeless and embarrassed, believing it was too late to learn after swallowing half the pool among eight-year-olds.

qa.q: What did Tarun learn about "yet" and effort?
qa.a: "Yet" opened the question of what to try next, but thrashing harder did not help; changing the method, with one-to-one sessions and floating first, is what worked.

qa.q: How might Tarun's sister feel hearing about the full length?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and pleased that her small word helped Tarun keep going.

grounding: It shows an adult replacing "I can't swim" with "I can't swim yet" and asking what to try next, while learning that effort needs a better strategy.

I share a flat with Ritu, and last month I watched her fight with bread.
She wanted to bake a proper loaf. The first one came out like a brick. She said, "I can't bake. I'm not a baking person," and nearly threw the flour away.
The next morning there was a sticky note on the fridge in her handwriting: I can't make bread YET. Below it, a list. Water too cold? Didn't knead long enough? Oven not hot enough?
I don't know what went on in her head. But she changed one thing each time. Warmer water. Longer kneading, with a timer. An oven thermometer she borrowed from me.
Loaf four was edible. Loaf six was actually good, and she gave me the heel with butter. The sticky note is still on the fridge. Someone, I think Ritu, has crossed out YET.

qa.a: Ritu borrowed an oven thermometer.

Jeevan did not submit his essay on Monday. When I asked, he showed me his notebook. The first page had been written, rubbed out and rewritten so many times that the paper had torn through in two places.
He said he had started the introduction nine times. "It wasn't good enough, ma'am. The first sentence has to be perfect or the whole essay is bad." He looked exhausted, and his hands were grey with eraser dust.
He is one of my strongest writers. I think he has set the bar so high that completing anything feels like losing.
I told him that a finished, imperfect draft gets more from me than a perfect sentence that never arrives. I asked for a rough draft by Wednesday, in pen, no erasing allowed, and promised feedback, not a grade.
He brought it on Wednesday. It was good.

I haven't told anyone this, not even Yogesh. I'm Imran, and I've been the "flawless" one since Class 5. Full marks, neat notebooks, teachers reading my answers aloud.
